title: Quantum random number generators
content_html:
Quantum random number generators

I Ching: yarrow stalks or coins. Mo: dice. In both cases, the physicality of the ritual matters: touching coins, invoking mantras, ritualised movements all add meaning. Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) exploit fundamental quantum indeterminacy (e.g., photon arrival times, radioactive decay). Unlike dice or coins, where unpredictability is practical (chaotic but deterministic), QRNGs produce numbers that are theoretically irreducible randomness - not computable in principle. Already used in cryptography, but they also open spiritual/artistic possibilities.

You can map QRNG outputs to the same structures - e.g., 0–63 → 64 hexagrams; 2–12 → mo dice outcomes. In traditional divination, randomness is mediated by ritual handling (embodied action), but with QRNGs, the “agency” shifts to cosmic physics itself - tapping into the ultimate indeterminacy of matter. Jung would see no issue - synchronicity does not require ritual handling, only meaningful coincidence. A QRNG output can be as synchronistic as a coin toss. QRNG randomness could be seen as a direct demonstration of śūnyatā (emptiness) and anicca (impermanence) at the quantum scale. It also resonates with the Tao as the ungraspable source - wu ji (無極, undifferentiated void) giving rise to yin–yang differentiation. Instead of physical ritual, the practice becomes a contemplative encounter with the void as generator of form.

Quantum random number generators offer a new medium for divination. They bypass human-made unpredictability and go straight to fundamental indeterminacy. Used with the I Ching or Tibetan mo, they can be read as a contemporary continuation of the same logic: patterns of chance as mirrors of mind and world.

Latency

A quantum random number generator (QRNG) API like ANU’s has some latency (hundreds of ms to a second or more). From a computational standpoint, this delay does not affect the statistical quality of randomness - once the numbers arrive, they are as irreducible and unpredictable as if measured instantaneously. In practice, the delay just slows down the interaction: instead of the result appearing immediately after you press “cast,” you wait briefly for the bits to arrive.

In traditional I Ching practice, using yarrow stalks or coins, the act itself takes time. The duration is not neutral: it is part of the contemplative space. Waiting for a QRNG response can serve a similar role - a pause that invites reflection, rather than a flaw. The latency becomes ritual time. In Buddhist or Daoist terms, timing is already interdependent: the moment of consultation is not a mechanical instant but a process unfolding. A slight network delay may even reinforce the idea that meaning is not in “perfect simultaneity” but in synchrony (Jung’s term).

The I Ching is less about “speed” and more about alignment - the casting event situates you in a web of change. Latency does not sever the link between your question and the outcome; it only re-frames it in a modern technological medium. Some might argue that latency reminds us that even in digital contexts, we cannot escape waiting and uncertainty - which itself resonates with the I Ching’s core message of impermanence and flux. If latency is very long (e.g., tens of seconds, or unreliable network), it could break concentration or feel like the ritual is “glitching.” This is more about user experience than metaphysics. Solutions include caching small pools of QRNG bits locally so that the felt flow is smooth.

Latency in QRNG services does not weaken the agency or validity of I Ching divination. If anything, the pause can be absorbed into the ritual space, much like shuffling, tossing coins, or handling yarrow stalks. The key is whether the practitioner frames the delay as part of the divinatory moment or as a frustrating technical hiccup.
